verses.verse:
विभागो लघुसंघातो विस्तारो लय योजला।
प्रवर्तनं हि तालेषु ततो गीतादिकल्पना।१४८।
verses.text: Division [of the scale], small clusters [of notes], elaboration, setting [them] in laya (tempo), and carrying [them] through the tālas; after that comes the composing of songs and the like.

commentary.text: Once the theoretical introduction has been gained, then by the rule of nature, first divide the ascent and descent of the rāga into the three saptakas (registers) and make small pieces in those notes, whose size is governed by mātrās (beats). After that, on the basis of those same groups of notes, let the rāga be elaborated by the rule of nyāsa (resting notes) and so on. Then, from that elaboration of notes free of laya (tempo), plan tāns (fast runs) bound to laya in full measure. Then carry those tāns through various tālas with the help of tempos such as dogun (double). Then at last the conception of a song or gat can succeed.

Material things too are usually made in this same order. For example, bricks from clay, walls from bricks, and a building from walls. Wood from a tree, and a bed and so on from wood. Flour from wheat, and bread (roṭī) from flour.

Now, following the rules in the śloka written above, first divide rāga Bhūpālī into the three saptakas (registers) and show small ascents and descents as follows. (1) Sa Ḍha P̣a, P̣a Ḍha Sa. (2) Sa Re Ga Pa, PaGa Re Sa. (3) Pa Dha Ṡa, ṠaDhaPa. (4) Ṡa Ṙe Ġa Ṗa, Ṗa Ġa Ṙe Ṡa.

Now some svarasaṅghātas (clusters of notes) of four mātrās each are being made on the basis of these same notes. It is hoped that practitioners (sādhakas) will reflect on the order of the following clusters and on their features, and in the same way will themselves make clusters of different numbers of mātrās in various rāgas, practising them in writing and in playing, and will become so skilled that in every musical composition they will see nothing but clusters. Then they will try out their own understanding in other rāgas too.

following.text: Bigger groups of notes can also be made by joining the small groups given above to one another. These can be used in any gat or song on the basis of the tāla. So that composing tāns (fast runs) bound to tāla, and practising them, becomes still easier, the help of words will be necessary for this ease. Then, notes bound in words are not forgotten. From those words we will also get the hint that the tongue (jībh, zubān) is to be used with the syllables: where one long syllable stands on several notes, the tongue will be used there on only one note, and the remaining notes will be expressed only by placing and lifting the finger. For example, if we play this group (PaDha Ṡa Dha Pa) without the help of words, then out of habit the tongue will be used on all the notes, like (ṭaṭa ṭā ṭā ṭā); and if it gets the support of words, the tongue will have to be used only on the letters standing in the words - PaDha Ṡa Dha Pa, mā- - dhapa pa, ṭā- - ṭā ṭā

The point is that for a note above or below which a syllable is written, the use of (ṭā) is proper; and a note below or above which the khaṇḍākāra mark (-) is written instead of a syllable should be made clear with the finger alone, without (ṭa). In the early period it is hard to carry out this action. To make this difficulty easy, one should practise for a long time in the form of alaṅkāras (patterned exercises), using many notes on one (ṭa) and many (ṭa) on one note. For example -
Many notes on one ṭa - Sa Re Ga Ma ṭā - - -
Many ṭa on one note - Sa Sa Sa Sa ṭa ṭa ṭa ṭa

If there is no success in this action, no song can be imitated or followed. If the svaralipi (notation) of a song reaches us in written form, and I also have exact knowledge of the signs of the notation, then we can sing that song according to that notation. But there will be full success in playing it on the flute and other suṣira vādyas (wind instruments) only when I can have correct control over the tongue as well, along with my phūṅk (breath into the flute) and fingers.

Groups of notes can be composed in other rāgas according to the rule given before. Then, by binding them in tāla with the help of some poem, a song or gat can be composed. Now a rāga can be mentioned for which the śāstra prescribes śuddha (natural) 'Ni' in the ascent and komal (flat) 'Ni' in the descent. To master this rāga there will be particular inconvenience with a six-hole flute. To remove that inconvenience, the practitioner should make more groups of notes like the following and practise them carefully and slowly, then play those same groups quickly. If possible, practise in single and double [tempo], and keep in mind that while playing ṆiSa the whole finger will be lifted. But while playing NiDha, for komal Ni the finger is to be lowered halfway or even less than halfway. If 'Dha' is varjit (omitted) in some rāga, then also practise separately lowering one and a half fingers to play komal Ni Pa.

following.text: By practising [in] 16 mātrās (beats), the ability to make tāns (fast runs) oneself can also come.

As you wish, you can play any two or more tāns by joining them one after another without a break. If, in each of the three parts of a tihāī, tāns of equal mātrās are joined and played in the proper number of mātrās, it will be called a camatkārik (astonishing) tān. Usually the same rule applies to cakkardār (circling) tāns too. For special knowledge, one should take refuge with a guru who is an expert in tāla.
